title: Ed Sheeran braces for pro-Palestine protest at Philadelphia concert
author: Our Foreign Staff
content:
![Ed Sheeran performs on stage during iHeartRadio z100's Jingle Ball 2025](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/09/19/TELEMMGLPICT000503697065_17898221166590_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqGYGDE_nezZAHzgJUlmrXn08FchWZRD3tSYOiRwPjWDo.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Ed Sheeran performs on stage during iHeartRadio z100's Jingle Ball 2025](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/09/19/TELEMMGLPICT000503697065_17898221166590_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqGYGDE_nezZAHzgJUlmrXn08FchWZRD3tSYOiRwPjWDo.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Pro-Palestine protests are expected outside Ed Sheeran’s concert on Saturday, his first show since his support acts quit in a row about the Gaza war.
Demonstrators are expected to congregate near Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia after Macklemore was dropped from Sheeran’s US tour for chanting “free Palestine” onstage in New Jersey this month.
City police said there would be an “appropriate police presence” to “help ensure the safety of concertgoers, employees and neighbourhood residents”.
Sheeran has denied being behind the decision to remove Macklemore after the owners of stadiums hosting forthcoming shows objected to the rapper’s presence in the line-up.
Four other supporting acts quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore and the Palestinian cause. They included Sheeran’s backing band as well as Finneas, the singer known for collaborating with his Grammy-winning sister Billie Eilish.
No new opening acts or backing bands have been announced. The rally is scheduled to take place in the afternoon.
![Ed Sheeran and Macklemore perform on stage](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/09/19/TELEMMGLPICT000503310534_17898217828300_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqCV9z637JvhpU71GNqQWVQrVK_UKM0aeUd4-4WL9bR_8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Tickets for the show have changed hands on the resale market at a slightly brisker pace since Monday than for previous dates on the tour, according to tracking site TicketData.
“Some share of the audience isn’t tuned in to anything political, or is completely indifferent to it, and has only just now become aware that Ed Sheeran is even playing their city. They’re buying tickets with zero connection to the controversy,” Keith Pagello, the site founder, said.
The price of the cheapest tickets had fallen from $123 on Monday to $54 by Saturday morning.
Mr Pagello said the decline was not necessarily linked to the row, as it is common for ticket prices to drop as the date of a concert approaches.
While a growing number of artists have spoken out against the conflict in Gaza and West Bank settler violence, Sheeran has maintained a apolitical stance.
“I am not complicit,” the 35-year-old British performer said on Instagram on Tuesday. “I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care.” However, he said: “Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum.”
summary: Ed Sheeran is facing a pro-Palestine protest outside his concert in Philadelphia following a controversy involving dropped and quitting supporting acts. Macklemore was removed from the tour after chanting "free Palestine" onstage, prompting four other acts to quit in solidarity, though Sheeran has denied making the decision to drop the rapper. Sheeran stated he maintains an apolitical stance for his shows, while Philadelphia police have planned an appropriate presence to ensure safety.
key_points: Pro-Palestine protests are expected outside Ed Sheeran's concert at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia.
Macklemore was dropped from the US tour after chanting "free Palestine" onstage, leading four other supporting acts to quit in solidarity.
Ed Sheeran denied being behind Macklemore's removal, noting that stadium owners objected to the rapper's presence.
Sheeran has maintained an apolitical stance for his concerts, stating that audiences do not expect a political forum.

title: New Strictly hosts make debut as first celebrity pairings revealed

content:

title: Johannes Radebe on Strictly and survival: ‘I was told I’d amount to nothing’
author: Lauren Morris
content:
I’ve been in the bottom of the pits and I’ve rubbed shoulders with the King and the Queen,” Johannes Radebe tells me. “I’m a boy from Zamdela who never thought life could possibly turn out this way.” He lets out a hearty laugh, shifting back – as he tends to do – into dazzle mode. “It did give me resilience, my darling.”
Tonight, Radebe will make his debut as one of three new presenters guiding viewers through the revamped Strictly Come Dancing, alongside Emma Willis and Josh Widdecombe. And he’s the only one with connecting tissue to the show’s earlier Tess-and-Claudia incarnation, having served as a professional dancer on Strictly since 2018. He admits he’s nervous, but he’s also made of strong stuff. Growing up in South Africa during the final years of apartheid, the 39-year-old withstood homophobia and a period of homelessness while pursuing a dance career in Johannesburg. Reading an autocue seems a cakewalk in comparison. Still…
“I want to lock myself up,” Radebe purrs, like Eartha Kitt. He’ll tune into tonight’s pre-taped launch show on his own. “I want to keep an open heart and mind because I’m my biggest critic. I don’t want to have opinions around me while I’m watching it. Afterwards, I’ll come out and face the world.”
Nerves aside, Radebe is otherwise giddy as we chat over Zoom. He is holed up in his London flat, still coming down from recording the first new Strictly a few days before we speak. The live shows – a whole other challenge in themselves – properly start next Saturday. Today, Radebe lives up to his warm reputation, and is just as elegant with his softly spoken answers as he is on the dance floor. It’s easy to see why mums across the nation have fallen for him. A powerful memoir and a celebrated run on the West End earlier this year, in Kinky Boots, couldn’t have hurt. He is, to put it succinctly, a star.
![Radebe with his new 'Strictly' co-hosts Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/09/18/14/40/576299.jpg)
So it’s no real surprise that he’s been tasked with captaining the Strictly ship into uncharted territory. As well as out of those choppy, scandal-infested waters. The show is entering its 24th series, its first in its history without Tess Daly, and its first without Claudia Winkleman in 12 years. The stakes have never been higher. Contrary to recent reports, though, presenting duties will be “evenly distributed” between Radebe, Willis and Widdecombe, who’ll be joined by a raft of celebrities – everyone from EastEnders’ Lacey Turner and Gavin & Stacey’s Melanie Walters to dog trainer Graeme Hall – also getting used to the new format.
For Radebe himself, his new job came as a surprise. Just months before he was asked to try out for it, he was contemplating his future with the show. “I had gotten to a point where I was like, ‘What’s next in my life?’” he explains. He remembers having long chats about it with his mother. “She said, ‘What are you thinking for 2026? Are you going to come back home? I’ve missed you.’ That’s the thing a lot of people don’t realise – I don’t live with my family because I am where I am. I’m alone. So, I’ve been craving time with them and seeing my niece and nephew grow up.”
Then there was the spectre of turning 40, which had already led him to think about slowing down on his dancing for his body’s sake. “My bones are tired, my bunions are tired,” he laughs. “I made it my life’s mission to find other opportunities outside of this.”
So how did he find himself up for such a huge promotion?
“Lauren, I don’t know myself!” he hoots.
What he does know is that he received a call early in the year from a Strictly producer, who asked whether he’d be interested in auditioning. “I was like, ‘Johannes, the thought of even saying yes to this opportunity – who the hell do you think you are?’” he says. “But they said, ‘We fully understand you’re not a broadcast or presenter. We know you are somebody who understands the fabric of the show. You love the show and we will guide you.’ If I didn’t have that conversation with him, I wouldn’t have even said yes to that chemistry test. But I also thought… nothing ventured, nothing gained. If anybody else had this opportunity, they would grab it with both hands, right? So why not me?”
![Radebe performing on ‘Strictly’ last year with celebrity partner Alex Kingston](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/03/03/15/20/SEI268985939.jpeg)
After various callbacks and chemistry readings, Radebe found out on a Zoom call that he’d be presenting the show with Widdicombe and Willis. “I screamed,” he grins. “I was alone in the apartment. I think my neighbours must have thought, ‘What is going on?’ But that’s how it played out.”
Since then, the trio have been bonding and swapping showbiz notes. Radebe has given them the lowdown on who’s who and what’s what at Strictly, while they’ve provided him with a crash course on comic timing and presenting. “That’s what got me through the launch show, honestly,” he gushes. “I think Emma held my hand throughout the whole process.”
But he knows that his time on Strictly could have ended very differently. With the show’s new format came a complete shake-up of the professional cast; Karen Hauer, Gorka Marquez and three other dancers moved on to make way for five fresh faces. It’s part of the reason Radebe was ready for change. “Our journey on the show as professional dancers is very short-lived,” he says. “I know people have come and gone and I know that it would have been [my] trajectory. But I’ve always said that if they got rid of me or if I ever stopped, I would [love to] come back and work as part of the crew, just to be part of the magic.”
The brutal nature of showbiz doesn’t faze Radebe, though, given everything he’s been through. He’s been open about the challenges he faced growing up in the mining town of Zamdela, raised by a supportive mother but a father who became violent with alcohol. A lover of Barbie dolls and his mother’s make-up, Radebe was a target of homophobia at school, which at times left him contemplating suicide. Later, he scraped together as much money as he could to live in Johannesburg, paying taxi drivers to sleep in the back of their cars or sneaking into the dance studio where he taught to stay overnight. After working on cruise ships for seven years, he was finally cast in the South African version of Strictly in 2014. Four years later, the UK Strictly came calling.
“I’m grateful now, looking back on everything I’ve been through,” he says. “The bad. The ugly … Because I wouldn’t appreciate what I have now if I didn’t go through all of that. It’s a blessing and a curse to know life in both extremes. I pinch myself every morning when I wake up, [knowing] that I’ve created a life I’ve always dreamt of.”
In his early dance days, Radebe was told by a rival that he wouldn’t “amount to anything” in life. He’s grateful to the UK – of which he became a citizen in February – for proving them wrong. “For a long time, I thought they were right. It took me until my thirties to realise they were wrong,” he says. “It took this country and being seen and appreciated and being championed the way I have in the past eight years for me to come to that realisation.”
Strictly has been one of TV’s biggest star-making machines for decades – which only really dawned on Radebe during his 2022 solo stage tour Freedom. Suffering from a bout of imposter syndrome, he was tempted to cancel beforehand. “I just thought to myself, who am I to think that I’m going to sell out theatres around this country?’” he recalls. “My agent said, ‘You don’t realise the impact you’ve had doing what you do and doing what you love.’ I thank God for that encouragement because I wouldn’t have done it honestly.” Radebe pauses. “He did also say to me, ‘If you pull out, our producers will sue us because we’ve signed a contract already.’ I was like, ‘Okay!’”
He still experiences those pangs of self-doubt, he says. But he’s better at dealing with them now. After all, just look at the material.
“I never thought I’d be an author, an actor, or a West End performer,” he says. “Now I’m presenting this show. I didn’t have this in my plans for my life. So I’ve got the tools to deal with imposter syndrome, and I’ve got proof to back it up.”
‘Strictly Come Dancing’ returns to BBC One tonight at 7.25pm
summary: Johannes Radebe is making his debut as a presenter on the 24th series of Strictly Come Dancing, joining Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe in the show's first major hosting shake-up in over a decade. Before landing the role, Radebe had been contemplating his future on the show due to his aging body and a desire to spend time with his family in South Africa. Despite facing severe hardship, homelessness, and homophobia growing up, Radebe has built a successful career as a dancer, author, and West End performer.
key_points: Johannes Radebe is one of three new presenters for the 24th series of Strictly Come Dancing, alongside Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe.
Radebe had originally been contemplating his future with the show and considering a break from dancing before being approached for the presenting role.
He brings resilience from a challenging upbringing in South Africa, which included surviving poverty, homelessness, and homophobia.
Radebe admits to experiencing nervousness and imposter syndrome regarding his new hosting duties, but he is supported by his co-hosts.

title: Claims Diana still ‘resented’ in Palace amid Earl Spencer book fallout - latest
author: Nicole Wootton-Cane
content:
Princess Diana is still “deeply resented” in Buckingham Palace, it has been claimed, as the fallout from Earl Spencer’s bombshell memoir continues.
Veteran broadcaster David Dimbleby told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that Diana’s refusal to act like other members of the royal family created tension in the Palace.
“She was fresh, new and exciting to the public and they really adored her,” Mr Dimbleby said. “And that was deeply resented in the palace. And still is. And this kind of tit for tat over who said what, and only two people know what was actually said just reignites all that”.
It comes after Earl Spencer claimed the late Queen reacted “tetchily” to the news that Diana had been in a car crash before she knew of its severity.
In the most recent extract from his memoir he said: “When the Queen had heard the first news of Diana being in a traffic accident, she had asked tetchily, ‘What is she up to now?’ This, before the seriousness of it all became clear.”
The Earl has insisted he is being truthful following backlash from Buckingham Palace, which said that the King is mindful that “grief can cloud reason”.
Earl's claims: Public reaction to Diana's divorce was 'main worry'
In an excerpt from his memoir, Earl Spencer has said that the public’s reaction was his “main worry” when Diana shared that she was getting a divorce.
In an extract from the bombshell book serialised by the Daily Mail, he described his conversation with Diana: "I was silent for a moment. I had known things were bad, but not this bad."
The earl said he then told his sister his "main worry" was the public because he worried that "they won't forgive you".
"They've bought into a fairytale, and I reckon they may well - wrongly - blame you for destroying their fantasy," he told her.
Charles Spencer’s book is Diana’s unfinished business – Harry’s documentary will finish it
As Buckingham Palace hits back at the claims of King Charles’s reaction to the death of Diana, Dan Wakeford, former People editor and founder of the Celebrity Intelligence website, looks at why her brother is publishing his tell-all now, and how the next 12 months will be about settling scores.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/18/10/45/harry-charles-spencer.jpeg?trim=0,0,0,0&width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
Charles Spencer’s Princess Diana memoir stolen from lorry
Copies of Charles Spencer’s new memoir about his sister Princess Diana have been stolen from a lorry ahead of its release date, according to reports.
The book, titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is set to be released globally next Tuesday (22 September) – but copies have been snatched from a lorry in the Netherlands, with Dutch police reportedly investigating the break-in.
A source told the Daily Mail: “It's extremely suspicious. Nothing like this has ever happened before. This is probably the biggest book of the year and the security surrounding it has been incredibly tight.”
You can read more below:
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/16/8/51/charles-spencer-diana.jpeg?trim=0,0,0,0&width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
Watch: King Charles issues rare response to Earl Spencer’s Diana book claims
Charles called Diana 'chubby' after engagement, claims Spencer's memoir
Diana suffered from an eating disorder which worsened after Charles called her “chubby,” Earl Spencer has claimed in his bombshell memoir.
In an extract from his book, serialised in the Daily Mail, the Earl claims that ahead of his sister’s wedding, Prince Charles had squeezed Diana’s waist and said, “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren't we?”
The earl said his sister found the comment "devastating," later telling him that her "waist shrank from 29 to 23 and a half inches between her engagement and her marriage," which were five months apart in 1981.
Royal expert suspects ‘collusion’ and ‘guilt’ behind Earl Spencer’s bombshell claims
A royal expert has shared his thoughts on the motivations behind Earl Spencer’s “brutal” claims against Buckingham Palace.
A war of words has broken out between the royal family and Princess Diana’s brother over allegations made in his upcoming memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister.
Revelations from the book, serialised by the Daily Mail before it is published on Tuesday (22 September), have so far focused on the King’s behaviour, from alleged statements he made to Diana before their marriage to the Earl's claims about comments the King made to him before her funeral.
Richard Fitzwilliams told The Independent he believes Earl Spencer is “haunted … by demons of himself” and that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex had some part to play.
”Timing all this just so happens it's just after Harry and Meghan have come back... The Sussexes, whether they actually saw the manuscript or what they knew about it, of course, I don't know. But I'm absolutely certain that there was some form of collusion or appears to have been.”
![](https://cdn.jwplayer.com/v2/media/7XsVsyGb/poster.jpg?width=720)
King 'sounded giddily elated’ after Diana's death, book claims
King Charles allegedly acted like a “lottery winner” in the hours after Princess Diana’s death, her brother Earl Spencer has claimed in his bombshell new memoir.
In the latest serialisation of the damning book, the then-Prince of Wales is accused of appearing “giddily elated” on the phone, shortly after his former wife had been killed in a car crash in Paris.
Earl Spencer has also revealed details about the couple’s unhappy marriage, and Diana’s wish to call off the engagement prior to their wedding in 1981.
Prince Charles ‘had no place at his his ex’s funeral’
Earl Spencer recalled his sister’s funeral as a “a form of mental torture,” stating that he believed neither Prince Charles, or Princes William and Harry should have been in attendance.
Sharing his feelings on the funeral procession, one passage read: “What was Prince Charles actually doing there? I thought at one moment.
“This ex-husband, from a marriage that had collapsed so bitterly four years before and finally ended in divorce a year earlier, surely had no place at his ex’s funeral.
“Supporting his sons was the reason given for his prominent place, but what were the boys doing there, anyway? It all seemed mad to me.
“I was anxious that I could not look sideways to check how Harry was doing. But at one point I found us marching briefly out of sight, under a massive arch. Relieved that nobody could see us here, I quickly leant across to Harry, and gave him an encouraging hug. ‘Well done, Harry!’ I said. ‘You’re doing bloody brilliantly!’”
How close was Charles Spencer to his sister Diana? Inside their complicated family bond
As Diana’s younger brother goes to war with the palace over incendiary revelations from his new book about his sister, Katie Rosseinsky takes a closer look at their sibling relationship, from a deep childhood connection to more friction and distance in later in life.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/17/15/57/Diana-and-brother_02-c838ed85.jpeg?trim=0,0,1847,0&width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
summary: Princess Diana's brother, Earl Spencer, has made controversial allegations against Buckingham Palace and King Charles in his upcoming memoir, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister." The book includes claims about Charles's past remarks to Diana, his reaction following her death, and tension over her public popularity. Meanwhile, copies of the highly anticipated memoir were recently stolen from a lorry in the Netherlands.
key_points: Earl Spencer claims in his memoir that Princess Diana's refusal to act like other royals caused deep resentment within Buckingham Palace that persists today.
The memoir alleges that Prince Charles called Diana "chubby" before their wedding, which worsened her eating disorder.
Earl Spencer claims King Charles sounded "giddily elated" on the phone hours after Diana's death.
Copies of the memoir were stolen from a lorry in the Netherlands ahead of its global release on 22 September.

title: ‘A maelstrom of his own making’: how Ed Sheeran’s tour turned into a full-blown culture war
author: Nadia Khomami
content:
Ed Sheeran has long been known as the “Mr Nice Guy” of music. His is an unthreatening kind of pop stardom; he looks and talks like the bloke who might be standing behind you in a pub, rather than someone selling out stadiums. He champions other artists, he celebrates different cultures. His songs are about love, heartbreak and friendship. People get engaged at his concerts.
But this week, one of the most successful musicians in the world faced the biggest controversy of his career, and found himself dragged into exactly the kind of political row he has spent his career avoiding.
It began when Macklemore, the Grammy-winning rapper supporting Sheeran on the US leg of his Loop tour, used his set at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey to call for a “free Palestine”. He performed Hind’s Hall, his 2024 protest song for a five-year-old girl killed by Israeli forces, while footage of pro-Palestine student demonstrations and destruction in Gaza played behind him.
The backlash was immediate. The StopAntisemitism group accused Macklemore of “ambushing” fans with “anti-Israel propaganda”, a post amplified by the singer Pink. The Israeli-American Council called for him to be pulled from the tour, asking where the line should be drawn “when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda”. There was extra heat given Macklemore’s history: in 2014 he performed in a fake beard, wig and prosthetic nose widely read as a Jewish caricature. He was soon dropped from the remaining tour dates.
But then Macklemore turned the story on Sheeran, accusing his friend of a “determination not to take sides publicly”, and claiming Robert Kraft – owner of the New England Patriots – had pressured Sheeran by threatening to pull his stadium from the tour dates and urging other venues to do the same. Sheeran’s team confirmed multiple venues had objected to Macklemore staying on the bill. Kraft, a prominent supporter of Israel and founder of the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism, has a personal relationship with Sheeran, who sang at his 2022 wedding. In a phone call with Sheeran, the billionaire reportedly acknowledged the sensitivity of Gaza but argued Macklemore’s remarks crossed into hate speech.
“Taking a side can cost you,” Macklemore said. “Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I’ve lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed.”
![Man with red hair and a checked shirt next to man with quiff dressed in black leather jacket, both in front of microphones](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/77dcd3dba91eefb7f7212db8cbde60b29ac0e1f3/0_0_3000_2285/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Sheeran’s own statement, published a day later, did little to calm things. He said dropping Macklemore was not his decision and he was “deeply disappointed” by it, but made clear he was not using the moment to declare a position on Israel and Palestine.
He was “appalled by the conflict”, he wrote, adding that the “suffering and pain caused on both sides” was “a human tragedy”. “I am not complicit. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have [personal views], and it doesn’t mean that I don’t care.” He wanted his concerts to stay places of “safety and sanctuary”, where people could gather regardless of politics.
![A woman in a beige overcoat and a man dressed in black paint a mural of a singer draped in red, green and white](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ae2a8c76f6af86bb2cf0b5b531136f21aba51e83/0_0_6720_4480/master/6720.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) was unconvinced: Sheeran’s statement, it said, “attempts to ‘both-sides’ Israel’s ongoing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza” and its appeal to “peace” left out “its crucial condition – justice”.
“The stakes for him would have been very, very high,” said Dorian Lynskey, the author of 33 Revolutions Per Minute: A History of Protest Songs. “Taking a stand meant potentially cancelling the rest of your tour, with all the refunds, people who work on the tour losing their work. It’s an enormous thing.”
![Man with short hair in T-shirt featuring red, white and blue lettering, smirks into lens.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3b70005c7c89c10319aabc7e5907ac74063236d8/919_0_3167_3167/master/3167.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Lynskey, who has interviewed Sheeran several times, has “a lot of sympathy” for him, but he thinks the attempt to frame the decision as something that simply happened around him, rather than a choice he made, has backfired. “He may end up being put in another position which is further away from where his sympathies lie. He’s now being seen as a supporter of genocide, when he obviously isn’t.”
Within days, every other support act on the US tour pulled out, including Finneas, Lukas Graham, the Irish band Beoga and Aaron Rowe. Sheeran’s Instagram following dropped by almost 150,000 in 24 hours; Macklemore gained more than 750,000. The actor Hannah Einbinder, Irish musician CMAT and Zara Larsson spoke up for Macklemore. Then Tommy Robinson tweeted his support for Sheeran, yanking the singer into a political camp about as far as possible from where he would want to be.
Suddenly, one rapper’s decision to speak from a concert stage had ballooned into a full-blown culture war. Many were asking: how does a man who has built a fortune on being liked by everyone end up here?
Subtly progressive
The answer partly lies in the distinction Sheeran has always drawn between having political views and making them part of his public identity. He has never been entirely apolitical. In 2017, he said he was supporting Jeremy Corbyn at the general election, while also saying he did not want to tell other people how to vote. He has campaigned on music education and copyright and supported charities including Crisis. In 2022, he performed at the Concert for Ukraine alongside other artists, raising more than £13.4m for humanitarian relief after Russia’s invasion.
Paloma Faith, who also played at the Concert for Ukraine, highlighted what she perceived as a hypocrisy. “He wasn’t apolitical by doing that and I don’t really understand why one felt more political than the other,” she told Channel 4 News.
![Woman with red baseball cap](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/64cfa4b7a6658d806ff1c9c8e4a0d47c3567ef04/0_0_6122_4017/master/6122.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The difference, said Lynskey, is that Ukraine reads in the west as a “consensus position” – “like Chris Martin wearing the pride flag, subtly progressive without risk of a massive backlash. That’s the realm Sheeran exists in: generally on the right side of things without talking about them too much. This time he’ll have had people around him going ‘this is how much money you lose’ or ‘this is how you could be tarred as antisemitic’.”
Musicians speaking out is nothing new, from Dylan and civil rights to punk and anti-apartheid – and neither is the price of doing so. In 2003, the Dixie Chicks faced boycotts, radio bans and death threats after Natalie Maines criticised George W Bush over Iraq. What sets Sheeran apart is that he did not say the controversial thing himself – someone he chose to put on his stage did. Choosing Macklemore was not the same as endorsing everything he says. But Macklemore’s politics are not incidental to who he is.
![Man in black flat cap and glasses with black overcoat](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/216eff41006e8b3ed1fde7c3113981ca9907e85b/403_0_3667_3667/master/3667.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“He can’t say: ‘I didn’t know Macklemore was going to do that’,” said Billy Bragg, who has spent decades making explicitly political music. “Macklemore has been speaking out about Palestine and the war in Gaza for quite some time now. His song Hind’s Hall and its accompanying video are a central aspect of his set. Ed’s people must have seen that on every other night of the tour.”
Stephen Millar, the author of Sounding Dissent, calls it “a maelstrom partly of Sheeran’s own making”. Sheeran had chosen an artist whose politics were well established, he said. “By doing that you could say that was his effort to the cause. But to pull that back is almost like wanting your cake and eating it.”
David Hesmondhalgh, a professor of media, music and culture at the University of Leeds, said while artists should not be compelled to take a position on everything, “Sheeran arguably gains credibility from associating himself with an act like Macklemore whose star persona is based on strong political commitments … So his declarations of neutrality look a bit spineless”.
‘A real S-storm’
The episode also points to a broader shift in what people expect of celebrities. Social media and the sheer weight of feeling over Gaza have made the old split between public image and private politics much harder to hold. “If you’re not using your platform, you’re seen as doing something wrong,” Millar said.
At the same time, artists have become proxies for arguments much bigger than themselves. Lynskey pointed to figures such as Gal Gadot and Mark Ruffalo, who have become stand-ins for opposing sides of the Israel-Palestine debate. “There is this sort of proxy war fought out with celebrities. People have been protesting for almost three years and it doesn’t seem to have made any difference, so I think they’re getting more and more angry and frustrated.”
The journalist Lulu Garcia-Navarro made a similar point to CNN: “There’s an increasing antipathy towards Israel, regardless of left or right, and popular culture gives people a way in – they’re not talking about what’s happening in Congress, but this they can understand.” She pointed to a second layer, too: “Both the left and right feel like they don’t have control over their free speech … today there’s a perception that pro-Palestinian voices get censored. So it’s become a real S-storm.”
![Woman with hair pulled back and a blue top in a train](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/af840cc6878189cd0a0d3a288d26ceba5cffe42e/0_0_1795_2000/master/1795.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Lisa Nandy, the UK culture secretary, said she had “enormous sympathy” for Sheeran, calling his position “really difficult and impossible” – he wanted to platform his support acts, she said, while promoters were warning himthey would cancel shows over politics on stage.
Bragg also acknowledged the practical realities. “Undoubtedly Ed has contractual obligations, and he’d get sued and it would cost him money,” he said. “I can understand it.” But he believes Sheeran could have drawn a cleaner line between defending Macklemore’s right to speak and endorsing every word of it.
“He doesn’t have to come out and say ‘free Palestine’. Put purely on the grounds of free speech, he can say an artist must be able to express their view. He needs to let people know how he feels about billionaires deciding what can and can’t be said from a stage,” he said.
“Of course, someone like Kanye West should be banned because of the antisemitic things he’s said. But drawing attention to the suffering of civilians in Gaza is not a reason to lose your gig. Culture has to entertain, but it can also challenge.”
The point found an echo on the American left. “When you see what Robert Kraft did, to line up all of the stadiums to censor speech in that one specific way, it’s become clear this isn’t about one or two music artists – it’s about how a handful of stadium owners and the elite can bury an entire massive issue. In this case, the genocide in Gaza,” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez told TMZ. “We need to be very clear about how dangerous a precedent this is.”
Lynskey worries about the wider lesson. “Are you just going to vet your support act for politics? Is the lesson that big artists learn that you don’t book anybody who might be a bit spicy? That would be terrible.”
Taking a stand
Sheeran is due back onstage at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday – with no support acts and no band. “I can’t think of a clear precedent where a star of that size has been put in that kind of situation because of support acts,” Lynskey said. It’s a sharp contrast to his last tour, one of the best-attended of all time; this time thousands of tickets sit unsold, some going for $65 online. Classic Hits Radio in Ireland has dropped him from its playlist “for the foreseeable future”, citing listener reaction.
![Man with a blue shirt performs on a stage bathed in pink light](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e779561c9ea0a4436a226b69ab146fdd46c1a6e6/736_209_7331_5169/master/7331.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“In Ireland, rebel songs were used to resist against British occupation for centuries, so the fact that Sheeran makes so much of his Irishness makes his stance all the more jarring,” Millar said.
Sheeran has tried to answer the controversy on his own terms: through money instead of words. Macklemore has pledged $1m of his Loop tour earnings to humanitarian organisations in Gaza; Sheeran and Kraft have each promised $2m for “aid in the region”. It is a way of showing he cares about the human cost without making any overt political statements – but whether it satisfies the people who wanted him to speak is another matter.
Paul Rieckhoff, the founder of Independent Veterans of America, who was inside MetLife Stadium with his two young children on the night of Macklemore’s statement, told CNN Sheeran might be better placed than most to do some good here: “Maybe Ed Sheeran is the person who can actually bring people together around this. But it’s not going to be by throwing Macklemore under the bus or by appeasing Bob Kraft.”
Bragg said: “By trying to be Mr Nice Guy and not take sides, he’s in danger of becoming a pariah himself. And that would be a shame, because it’s not his fault. He does need to make a choice here, and it’s one I think that will define him in the eyes of the public for a long time.”
summary: Ed Sheeran faced a major controversy during his US tour after his opening act, Macklemore, performed a pro-Palestine song and was subsequently dropped from the lineup following backlash. While Macklemore and critics accused Sheeran of caving to pressure and avoiding taking a side, Sheeran stated he wanted his concerts to remain neutral places of sanctuary. The incident sparked a wider culture war over celebrity political expression, free speech, and the Israel-Hamas conflict.
key_points: Macklemore used his set on Ed Sheeran's US tour to call for a "free Palestine" and perform a protest song, leading to immediate backlash and his removal from future tour dates.
Macklemore and other critics claimed billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft pressured Sheeran into dropping the rapper, though venues had widely objected to the political remarks.
Sheeran released a statement expressing disappointment over Macklemore's removal while maintaining his own neutrality and calling the conflict a human tragedy.
The controversy caused all other support acts to pull out of the tour, resulted in a drop in Sheeran's social media followers, and drew conflicting reactions from politicians and musicians.
Commentators noted the event highlights a growing expectation for celebrities to take public political stances, transforming pop tours into proxies for broader geopolitical debates.

title: Earl Spencer's Diana book opens old wounds royals would rather forget
author: Sean Coughlan
content:
![Diana, The Princess Of Wales Visits Washington, USA for a Gala Dinner held by The American Red Cross, to raise funds for landmine victims around the world.  1997](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/dc52/live/508ec510-b377-11f1-9023-9990160baacc.jpg)
- Published
The legacy of the shocking death of Diana, Princess of Wales, is still the rawest of wounds for the royals, as demonstrated by the no-holds-barred memoir from her brother Earl Spencer.
It might be almost 30 years ago, but Buckingham Palace's unusually angry rebuttal to the book's allegations of a callous response to his ex-wife's death from the then Prince Charles shows how much this still matters.
That late summer in 1997 was a moment when the Royal Family looked out of touch, lacking in empathy for Diana's loss, and at peril of losing public support, as people laid siege to the palaces with flowers.
While the royals dealt with their own private grief, they were also facing a reputational disaster, at risk of becoming the focus of public dismay at the sudden death of the "People's Princess" in a car crash in Paris.
![A multi-coloured sea of floral tributes to Diana, Princess of Wales, lie outside the gates of her London home.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/1df2/live/24a35f50-b378-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
An outpouring of public grief saw flowers laid outside palaces and Diana's homes
"It was a very febrile mood. Everyone was taken by surprise by the strength of feeling, and the strength to which the Royal Family was unpopular. The palaces were deemed to have treated Diana badly," recalls royal author Valentine Low.
Low was inside Westminster Abbey for Diana's funeral and vividly remembers the public response to the electrifying speech made by Earl Spencer.
"I heard this noise. I couldn't quite make out what it was, and then I worked out it was the crowd outside the abbey, who'd been listening on the speakers," he says.
"That noise appeared to come through the stone walls of the abbey and it was the most extraordinary thing - as people then started to applaud inside the abbey. It was so astounding, in front of Charles and all of the Royal Family."
A volatile public mood followed Diana's death, with the late Queen Elizabeth eventually having to respond with a live televised address paying tribute to the princess and acknowledging how difficult it can be to articulate grief.
"We have all been trying in our different ways to cope. It is not easy to express a sense of loss, since the initial shock is often succeeded by a mixture of other feelings: disbelief, incomprehension, anger - and concern for those who remain," said the late Queen.
A fresh-faced new prime minister, Tony Blair, was said to have been a modernising influence on sending such a direct message - an intervention later depicted in the movie, The Queen, starring Helen Mirren.
![Earl Spencer, Prince William, Prince Harry, Prince Charles and the Duke of Edinburgh follow the coffin to the funeral cortege of Diana, Princess of Wales as it arrives at Westminster Abbey on September 6, 1997 in London, England.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/3606/live/ece31060-b377-11f1-9023-9990160baacc.jpg)
There was disagreement about whether it was right for the princes to walk behind Diana's coffin
So many of the current tensions in the royal world can be traced back to the trauma of those events. The death of a mother at such a young age was inevitably a huge shaping influence on her sons - and it can feel as though those unresolved tensions are still playing out.
In the Duke of Sussex's memoir Spare, Diana's absence is a huge presence, his sense of loss unabated. There is still a graphic sense of his distress at walking behind her coffin, with Prince Harry mentioning Earl Spencer's opposition.
"Mummy's brother, Uncle Charles, raised hell. 'You can't make these boys walk behind their mother's coffin! It's barbaric'," wrote Harry.
Harry's accusation that the interests of the institution of the monarchy had been put above the happiness of individuals has been part of the narrative that saw him stepping down as a working royal and remaining at loggerheads with his brother, Prince William.
![The Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, speaking at her funeral at Westminster Abbey 06 September.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/704/cpsprodpb/a1de/live/8757ea20-b374-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
There was a wave of applause from outside Westminster Abbey when Earl Spencer finished his eulogy
The disputes that followed Diana's death, within the family and between in-laws, are still being aired loudly in Earl Spencer's book - Swan Song: Diana, My Sister - and in the global news coverage it has triggered. It opens up old questions about King Charles's character, his treatment of the young princess and his relationship with the now Queen Camilla.
On social media, Diana's fans are believing Earl Spencer's version of events, says Prof Pauline Maclaran of Royal Holloway, University of London. She says the royals remain "highly vulnerable" to anything that evokes the story of a "beautiful princess whose life was cut short in such tragic and ambiguous circumstances".
Royal commentator Jenny Bond described it as a "fantastically hostile, absolutely rude book... it's a very unpleasant portrayal of a man - but it's his memory of it, and who knows who's right?"
![Charles Spencer, 9th Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales (1961-1997), and her sons, Prince William and Prince Harry, attending the Princess's funeral service at Westminster Abbey, London, England, 6th September 1997.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/df22/live/fcf8d460-b374-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
Prince William was 15 and Prince Harry just 12 at their mother's funeral
At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Spencer: "We'll forget her soon enough."
He is accused of sounding "giddily elated" and like a "lottery winner" after the news of her death.
Buckingham Palace hit back with a response, which although dressed in courtier-like politeness, was essentially saying the conversation had never happened like that.
The King was said to be "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways that others do not recognise".
Anyone who has lost someone knows how feelings can run high, people can hear different things about the same conversations - and families can fall out, or come together, in the wake of a death.
Psychotherapist Nick Hatter says he doesn't have a view on which version of events is correct, but he says that during traumatic events memories can be "distorted". A phone call doesn't have any of the visual clues or body language to give a fuller picture, he adds.
Hatter says there can be very different and unpredictable responses to grief, including a condition known as "bereavement mania" where someone can seem inappropriately hyper or even euphoric after the loss of a loved one.
The first opinion poll on who to believe has been published by YouGov - and it suggests a very split view, with 31% believing Earl Spencer's allegations, 36% suspecting it's not true and 33% saying they don't know.
Low thinks the book is unlikely to change many opinions, as "people have settled into their camps about how they regard Charles, how they look back on the Diana years".
There could also be a feeling that it's "tawdry" to rake up these claims so many years later, he says.
That's echoed by historian and author Sir Anthony Seldon who says Earl Spencer showed great courage at the time of Diana's funeral, but says his memoir is a "sad and unnecessary publication".
Royal commentator Richard Palmer says the book threatens to take the royals back to the difficult days of 1997.
"This book and the run-up to next year's 30th anniversary of Diana's death threaten to undermine the Royal Household's three decades of work to rehabilitate Charles and Camilla's image," he says.
![King Charles III (then Prince Charles, the Prince of Wales), Lady Jane Fellows (left) and Lady Sarah McCorquodale with officials at RAF Northolt to meet the coffin of Diana Princess of Wales, as it arrives from Paris where she was killed in a car crash, 31st August 1997.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/1217/live/bf29a8c0-b375-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
King Charles walks with Diana's sisters Lady Jane Fellows (left) and Lady Sarah McCorquodale to meet her coffin as it arrives in England
Earl Spencer, in a statement ahead of the book's launch, said he had been "inundated" with requests for interviews about his sister, with the upcoming 30th anniversary prompting him to write down his own memories "rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths that have become accepted over time".
He is fiercely defending the accuracy of his claims, in interviews over the weekend, including with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.
In it Earl Spencer doubles down on his allegations about King Charles, saying: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.
"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."
Watch: Earl Spencer says he's 'telling the truth' about what Charles said after Diana died
In person, Earl Spencer is a very affable and charming figure, a writer who has had a first-hand view of some big royal moments and has the stories, sometimes scandalous, to show for it.
What makes his claims more potentially damaging is that he isn't writing as a pundit or commentator, but as someone who was sitting around the table with his in-laws and his own sister. It's a close up, emotional, insider's view, not a long lens and a headline.
If this book shows that the royals haven't escaped the legacy of Diana's death, then it also shows that neither has he.
You can watch Earl Spencer's interview with Laura Kuenssberg on Sunday from 16:00 BST on BBC iPlayer and on BBC One at 18:30.
![Thin, purple banner promoting the Royal Watch newsletter with text saying, âInsider stories and expert analysis in your inbox every weekâ. There is also a graphic of a fleur-de-lis in white.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/ef34/live/a99f61b0-109d-11f0-b234-07dc7691c360.png)
summary: Earl Spencer's memoir regarding the death of Diana, Princess of Wales, has reopened deep historical wounds and provoked an angry rebuttal from Buckingham Palace. The book alleges that the then Prince Charles made callous remarks following Diana's 1997 car crash, claims that the King's camp denies. Commentators note that the publication threatens decades of work by the Royal Household to rehabilitate the images of Charles and Camilla as the 30th anniversary of Diana's death approaches.
key_points: Earl Spencer's memoir contains allegations that the then Prince Charles responded callously to Diana's death during a phone call.
Buckingham Palace issued an unusual rebuttal, suggesting that grief and trauma can cloud memory and that the conversation did not happen as claimed.
A YouGov poll shows public opinion is split on whether to believe the allegations in the book.
Experts suggest the book threatens to undermine three decades of work by the Royal Household to rehabilitate the public images of King Charles and Queen Camilla.

title: Earl Spencer doubles down on claims about ‘monstrous’ call with Charles after Diana’s death
author: Sammy Gecsoyler
content:
Earl Spencer has doubled down on his bombshell claim that King Charles said of Diana, Princess of Wales, “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough” days after her death, saying he is telling the truth.
The alleged comments, revealed in Charles Spencer’s memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is being serialised in the Daily Mail, prompted Buckingham Palace to issue an extraordinary statement suggesting Diana’s brother had misremembered events, saying “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise”.
In an interview with the BBC, Spencer stood firm in his recollection, telling Laura Kuenssberg: “I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.”
Responding to the palace’s statement, Spencer said: “Well, is he furious? Is he furious, or is he embarrassed?” When asked about the inference that his memory was coloured, Spencer said: “They’ve sort of smudged that one, haven’t they? They’ve said that recollections may vary.”
![Diana in a black dress](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/58eb8b6f02366b460566624db559654e59e9935e/24_0_1263_1010/master/1263.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Spencer said the call was one of two he had with Charles in his lifetime and said he told his friends and family members at the time about the comment “because it was so monstrous”.
The alleged comment was revealed on Wednesday in an extract from the memoir published in the Daily Mail. The comment by the then prince was allegedly made during a heated argument over funeral arrangements. Spencer says it reflected Charles’s “pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death”, the Daily Mail reported.
Among other claims in the book are that Diana told a friend on the eve of her wedding to Charles that he said he was happy to marry her, but was not actually in love with her.
On Friday, the second extract from the memoir was published. Spencer writes Charles was “polite and formal” on the day of Diana’s funeral and says Prince Philip told him to look ahead while walking in unison alongside his nephews and former brother-in-law.
“It was hellish, entering that tunnel of grief, particularly because we were unable to put a face to it by looking at the individuals in the crowd,” said Spencer of the procession.
![Philip, William, Spencer, Harry and Charles walking in Diana’s funeral procession](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/98d10d9ba6c084602d253de85e618dacc1a206a5/114_0_1728_1382/master/1728.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In the extract released on Wednesday, Spencer says he insisted to Charles that Diana would not have wanted her sons, Prince William, then 15, and Prince Harry, then 12, to walk in her funeral procession. In the end, her sons walked behind her coffin, which William later called “one of the hardest things I’ve ever done”.
Spencer wrote that when one of Queen Elizabeth’s most senior aides told him in the days before the funeral that William and Harry would take part in the procession, he responded: “That’s not going to happen.”
after newsletter promotion
But minutes later he received a phone call from Charles, who insisted it should. It was during the ensuing argument between the two men that Charles allegedly made the comment, with Spencer writing: “‘Rest assured,’” he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’”
Spencer wrote that he was stunned and took a few seconds to reply, writing: “‘I can’t believe you just said that,’ I said flatly, before hanging up.”
Spencer also claimed that Diana “never would have wanted” her sons to walk behind her coffin, to which Charles allegedly replied: “That’s the problem with your family. They’ve got no bloody sense of duty.”
Swan Song is due to be published globally next Tuesday – in the UK by Penguin Michael Joseph, a division of Penguin Random House.
Four copies of the Dutch-language edition were reportedly taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher’s printers to their warehouse in the Netherlands.
Diana, who died aged 36 after a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year.
Buckingham Palace did not issue a statement responding to the BBC interview, but on Wednesday a spokesperson said: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”
summary: Earl Spencer is standing by claims made in his upcoming memoir that King Charles made a callous remark about Princess Diana shortly after her death. Buckingham Palace suggested in a statement that Spencer's grief has clouded his memory, but Spencer maintains he is telling the truth and recalled the conversation to friends and family at the time. The book also details disputes over the funeral arrangements, including the decision for Princes William and Harry to walk behind their mother's coffin.
key_points: Earl Spencer claims King Charles told him "rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough" during a phone call following Diana's death.
Buckingham Palace responded by stating that fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment, and colour memory.
Spencer insisted in a BBC interview that his recollection of the call is completely accurate.
The memoir alleges the disputed comment occurred during a heated argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

title: David Walliams' Fully Dropped By HarperCollins; Change To TV Agent
author: Jake Kanter
content:
![David Walliams](https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/GettyImages-1506862443-e1749722067693.jpg?w=681&h=383&crop=1) 
HarperCollins will stop publishing comedian David Walliams‘ back catalog of books, while Deadline understands that talent agency YMU is no longer actively representing the Little Britain star.
The Rupert Murdoch-owned publishing house initially dropped Walliams last year following misconduct allegations, but has now confirmed that it will no longer represent his backlist. The decision was first reported by The Bookseller.
Walliams, who has written bestselling children’s books like Gangsta Granny and Mr Stink, has denied wrongdoing. Deadline has approached Walliams’ literary agent for comment. Independent Talent Group continues to oversee Walliams’ literary interests.
Watch on Deadline
Separately, YMU is no longer actively representing the comedian and his profile has been removed from the company’s website. A source said Walliams “is not currently in a commercial relationship with YMU” following amicable talks in early 2026. YMU has not severed ties with Walliams having previously represented his TV interests, including his time as a judge on Britain’s Got Talent.
In December 2025, The Daily Telegraph reported that Walliams was the subject of an internal investigation the previous year regarding his alleged behavior towards junior female HarperCollins employees.
The newspaper reported that Walliams was accused of harassing the young women, with one staffer receiving a “five-figure payoff” after raising concerns. Former HarperCollins employees alleged that they were told to work with Walliams, 54, in “pairs” and were advised not to visit his home.
In a statement to The Telegraph, his spokesperson said: “David has never been informed of any allegations raised against him by HarperCollins. He was not party to any investigation or given any opportunity to answer questions. David strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately and is taking legal advice.”
Walliams is an established presence on British television and beyond, having created and co-starred in Little Britain with Matt Lucas in the noughties. They have made attempts to revive the BBC comedy and even spoke to Netflix about a new series in 2020.
Walliams has appeared in series, including Doctor Who and Agatha Christie adaptation Partners in Crime, and had roles in movies, including Murder Mystery and Stardust.
He served as a judge on Britain’s Got Talent for a decade alongside Simon Cowell, but left the show under a cloud after comments he made about contestants were leaked to The Guardian in 2022. In one example, he called someone a “c***.” Walliams later apologized for his comments.
summary: Publisher HarperCollins has decided to stop publishing comedian David Walliams' back catalog of books following misconduct allegations. Additionally, talent agency YMU is no longer actively representing him following amicable talks. Walliams, who was previously the subject of an internal investigation regarding alleged behavior toward junior female employees, has strongly denied any wrongdoing.
key_points: HarperCollins is no longer publishing David Walliams' back catalog of books.
Talent agency YMU is no longer actively representing Walliams following talks in early 2026.
Walliams was previously the subject of an internal investigation concerning alleged misconduct toward junior female HarperCollins employees.
Walliams has strongly denied all allegations of inappropriate behavior and is taking legal advice.

title: Stephanie Cole, Coronation Street and Open All Hours actor, dies aged 84
author: PA Media; Guardian staff reporter
content:
The actor Stephanie Cole, best known for roles in Coronation Street, Waiting for God and Open All Hours, has died aged 84.
She also appeared in the prisoner-of-war drama Tenko, A Bit of a Do and Doc Martin.
A statement from her agent, John Grant, on behalf of her family, said: “It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of Stephanie Cole, OBE.
“She passed away this morning at the age of 84. Stephanie had been living with Alzheimer’s disease for some years.
“Stephanie was an extraordinary talent whose long and distinguished career included many iconic performances in theatre and television. She brought joy to millions through her many much-loved roles in sitcom and drama.
“She will also be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities. During this incredibly difficult time, the family kindly requests privacy.”
![Cole sitting at a kitchen table reading a magazine, alongside her fictional son Roy Cropper and his wife, Hayley Cropper](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6cdbfc6bcfdd61b73df97390f22578717a61ec99/37_0_1959_1339/master/1959.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Cole appeared on Coronation Street between 2011 and 2013 as Sylvia Goodwin, the mother of Roy Cropper. She won the British Soap award for best comedy performance for the role.
Her other notable performances included roles in Still Open All Hours, in which she reprised her Open All Hours character Mrs Featherstone, The Cleaner, Gentleman Jack and Talking Heads: Soldiering On.
She won the British Comedy award for best actress for the 1990s sitcom Waiting for God, about residents of a retirement home.
Cole also had an extensive career in the theatre, with roles in King Lear, A Passionate Woman and Noises Off.
summary: Renowned actor Stephanie Cole, famous for her roles in Coronation Street, Waiting for God, and Open All Hours, has died at the age of 84. Her agent announced that she passed away after living with Alzheimer's disease for several years. Throughout her long and distinguished career, Cole brought joy to millions through iconic performances in television and theatre, and also supported mental health charities.
key_points: Actor Stephanie Cole died at the age of 84 after living with Alzheimer's disease.
She was best known for her television roles in Coronation Street, Waiting for God, and Open All Hours.
Cole won a British Soap Award for best comedy performance and a British Comedy Award for best actress.
Her extensive career included notable performances in both television sitcoms/dramas and the theatre.

title: Ed Sheeran backlash continues as radio station bans songs and Instagram fans unfollow
author: David Mouriquand
content:
Ed Sheeran’s turbulent week continues. His music has been pulled from a major Irish radio station and his Instagram followers are leaving him. The fallout from his US tour controversy grows, as the singer is due to return to the stage tomorrow – minus his touring musicians and opening acts.
Rare have downfalls been so spectacular, and for an artist who says he refuses to be drawn into political debate, Ed Sheeran has become a political lightning rod in a snowballing controversy which shows no signs of slowing down.
The British singer's once-wholesome image has taken an almighty nosedive following the dismissal of Macklemore from his US tour after venues objected to the rapper's outspoken support for Palestine.
After a very ill-advised PR statement - which did more damage to Sheeran's brand than anything else – and all of the singer's opening acts quitting in solidarity with Macklemore, Ed has faced a reputation-staining backlash. This includes calls for boycott and criticism from major figures in the music world and beyond.
Commentators have called him "spineless" and a "lowlife coward"; former Pink Floyd Roger Waters has dismissed him as a "prick"; and Massive Attack reminded Sheeran that "‘Neutrality’ in the face of the slaughter of more than 20,000 children can never be neutrality.”
Then came New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who argued the controversy was bigger than either performer, framing it as an example of powerful interests allegedly being able to silence artists who speak on political issues. Still, she admitted to TMZ that she would switch radio stations if a Sheeran song came on... And one radio station won't be an issue in this regard...
One of Ireland’s biggest commercial radio networks has announced that it is pulling Sheeran's music from its playlists - just hours before he is due back on stage in Philadelphia for his first show since he was left without 'A Team'.
Classic Hits Radio announced it would stop playing Sheeran's songs following feedback from listeners.
“Our decision to remove Ed Sheeran’s music from the Classic Hits Radio playlist has been carefully considered,” Dave Kelly, group programme director at Bay Broadcasting, which runs the radio station, said in a statement. “It is not intended as a personal judgment on Ed Sheeran, and we acknowledge his own explanation of the circumstances surrounding recent events.”
The station said it had also taken into account the decisions of Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, who withdrew from Sheeran's tour.
“As an independent Irish-owned radio station, however, we believe it is important to listen to our audience and to stand alongside Irish artists who have made what is undoubtedly a significant professional decision based on their own convictions,” Kelly said.
“Ultimately, our position is a simple one. We believe in peace, humanity and respect, and in the right of people and artists to express and act upon their sincerely held views."
Although Sheeran was born and raised in England, he has strong Irish family connections through his father and grandparents and has spoken publicly about his Irish heritage.
Previously, Rowe said that Sheeran had been a friend to him, “but as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation”.
“I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children. I would lose all respect for myself to carry on as normal.”
Beoga stated on Instagram that they would no longer be a part of Sheeran’s band “following the silencing of Macklemore by zionist lobbies”. They added that while they have been friends with Sheeran for over 10 years and will continue to be, “to play in venues that silence anyone advocating for Free Palestine is simply not an option for us”.
Elsewhere, the fallout has extended to Sheeran's social media accounts, as the singer's Instagram follower count is tumbling.
According to social media analytics company Social Blade, Sheeran lost 149,636 followers on Instagram in the day following Macklemore’s dismissal, while the rapper gained 750,098 followers during the same period.
In the space of three days, Sheeran has lost more than 260,000 followers, while Mackelmore and the artists have quit his tour have gained a combined 1.638 million.
Sheeran is due to perform at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia on Saturday – which will be his first time back on stage since the controversy spiralled. As of writing, no news on whether Sheeran will have new opening acts or if he'll perform alone.

summary: Ed Sheeran is facing a severe backlash and losing social media followers following the dismissal of rapper Macklemore from his US tour due to venues objecting to Macklemore's support for Palestine. In response to the controversy, opening acts and touring musicians have quit, and an Irish radio station has pulled Sheeran's music from its playlists. The singer is scheduled to return to the stage in Philadelphia without his original opening acts and band.
key_points: Ed Sheeran's music was pulled from Classic Hits Radio in Ireland following listener feedback and the withdrawal of Irish acts from his tour.
Macklemore was dismissed from Sheeran's US tour after venues objected to his support for Palestine, prompting opening acts to quit in solidarity.
Sheeran lost over 260,000 Instagram followers in three days following the controversy.
The singer faces widespread criticism from musicians, commentators, and politicians as he prepares to perform his first show since the fallout began.

title: Sway: Award-winning British rapper dies aged 44
author: Mark Savage
content:
![Sway wearing a blue cap and white shirt with his hands clasped in front of him](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/774b/live/fd00ea80-b34f-11f1-b949-71f91f81d1ab.jpg)
- Published
The award-winning British-Ghanaian rap artist Sway DaSafo has died at the age of 44.
He was the first unsigned rapper to win a Mobo Award in 2006, and scored a top 10 hit in 2012 with the single Level Up.
The news was first shared online by the Mobo organisation, and confirmed to the BBC by the musician's friend Kash Ahmad, who said he died at his home in Ghana.
No cause of death has been announced.
Sway was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma in 2010 and went into remission later that year.
'Positive person'
Sway was born Derek Andrew Safo in London, albeit accidentally, while his mother was on a stop-over between Amsterdam and her native Ghana.
After a brief period in her homeland, he was raised in north London and honed his craft on pirate radio. He credited the BBC's radio station 1Xtra with providing him with his first break in 2002.
Emerging during the first wave of grime, alongside artists such as Dizzee Rascal and Lethal Bizzle, he stood apart for his witty, literate style.
"I'm a positive person. The positivity comes out in my music," he told the Guardian as his career took off.
"I don't go round holding guns to people's heads so I won't rap about holding guns to people's heads."
Despite widespread interest from the music industry, he remained independent - releasing music on his own label, and selling mixtapes at markets and independent record shops.
He made headlines in September 2005 when he was named best hip-hop act at the Mobo awards - defeating US heavyweights such as 50 Cent and the Game.
![Sway at the 2006 Mobo Awards](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/b11a/live/72f5cf20-b2b6-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
In his early years, the musician often kept his identity hidden
The following year, he released his debut album This Is My Demo, accompanied by the top 40 single, Little Derek, which celebrated how he had "ended up in HMV instead of HMP".
Although the album stalled at number 78 in the charts, it earned him a nomination for the Mercury Prize, alongside acts like Arctic Monkeys and Muse.
In 2006, he supported The Streets on a UK tour and appeared alongside frontman Mike Skinner on the Mitchell Brothers' single Harvey Nicks.
Cancer diagnosis
But in 2010, DaSafo was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma.
"It felt like I had been dropped in the middle of the sea with no lifejacket," he later recalled.
"I didn't have time to think about how I was going to get to the other side, I just had to deal with it."
After receiving chemotherapy and radiotherapy, he went into remission, releasing his biggest hits Still Speedin' (which sampled Black Box's Ride On Time) and Level Up (featuring a verse from Kano) in 2012.
He enjoyed further critical and commercial success with albums including Deliverance, and Verses from the Vault; and collaborated with artists like Mark Ronson, Ed Sheeran, Akon and Childish Gambino.
Through his record label Dcypha, he also signed and developed artists including Tiggs Da Author and KSI.
All three appeared on the 2013 single No Sleep, and KSI went on to become a hugely successful YouTuber, with a sideline in music.
DaSafo also dabbled with an acting career, appearing in two episodes of the crime drama Top Boy and the 2012 film The Grind.
At the time of his death, he was working on new music. His final Instagram post, shared last week, external, celebrated his 44th birthday.
He is survived by two sons, Jalil and Ammar-Joseph, and twin daughters, Queen-Inaya and Queen-Imara. At the time of his death, he was raising them as a single parent in Ghana, his friend Kash Ahmad told BBC News.
"It was an honour and a pleasure to have known and worked with him, and my thoughts and prayers are with his family," he added.
Other tributes came from the Mitchell Brothers, who wrote: "We were privileged to have worked with you", and praised Sway's "true penmanship level and delivery".
![Sway attends the 2006 Mercury Music Prize](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/09bf/live/4c0c42e0-b2b6-11f1-819c-176371125270.jpg)
The musician was nominated for the Mercury Prize for his debut album, This Is My Demo
"This hit me like a ton of bricks," said rapper and record label executive Kardinal Offishall. "Rest in eternal peace and God cover your babies. Til we meet again my friend."
So Solid Crew's Megaman simply posted "RIP"; while The Mobo Awards said they were "proud to have him as part of our history," adding: "Our love goes out to his family, loved ones and fans."
Rapper Baby Blue posted on Instagram: "In my heart I worried this day was coming but I wasn't prepared for the reality of losing Sway.
"He was my confidante and he guided me through so much of my life musically and personally... I will miss you forever my friend. I am lost."
Breaking the news to her listeners on BBC Radio 1Xtra, broadcaster Remi Burgz said it was a "sad day for British music" and called Sway a "UK Rap pioneer".
"One of north London's finest," she said, "he was mine and many others first experience of UK rap [and] hip-hop in mainstream media".
"He was a literal example of paving the way and showing that UK rap can take up space in music.
"Rest in perfect peace to Sway."
summary: Award-winning British-Ghanaian rapper Sway DaSafo has died at the age of 44 at his home in Ghana, with no cause of death announced. He was a pioneering independent artist who made history in 2005 as the first unsigned rapper to win a Mobo Award, defeating major US heavyweights. Throughout his career, he achieved commercial success with hits like Level Up, earned a Mercury Prize nomination, and later raised his four children as a single parent in Ghana.
key_points: Sway DaSafo died at his home in Ghana at the age of 44, with no cause of death announced.
He made history in 2005 by becoming the first unsigned rapper to win a Mobo Award.
He was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma in 2010 but went into remission later that year following treatment.
His notable musical achievements include his Mercury Prize-nominated debut album This Is My Demo and the 2012 top 10 hit Level Up.
He is survived by his two sons and twin daughters.

title: Millie Bobby Brown reportedly welcomes second baby with husband Jake Bongiovi
author: Stefania Sarrubba
content:
Stranger Things and Enola Holmes star Millie Bobby Brown has reportedly welcomed her second child with husband Jake Bongiovi.
People has reported that the couple have adopted a second child. No further details are available at this stage, though a recent Instagram post from Brown might've given away that the family had expanded.
Taking to the social platform, the actor posted a carousel from a family vacation in the Dolomites mountain region of Italy. In a sweet clip, Brown can be seen holding her first daughter in her arms, while Bongiovi walks alongside them and two alpacas while wearing a baby carrier strapped to his chest.
The happy family give their backs to the camera, so that the newest addition isn't visible.
Fans of Brown also seem to think that one of the pictures she posted, depicting four eggs in a bowl, could hint at having a new baby in the family.
Digital Spy has reached out to Brown's representatives for comment.
Last year, Brown first announced that she and Bongiovi, who had tied the knot in 2024, had welcomed a child through adoption.
"This summer we welcomed our sweet baby girl through adoption. We are beyond excited to embark on this beautiful next chapter of parenthood in both peace and privacy," the star wrote in an Instagram post in August 2025. "And then there were 3."
Related: Millie Bobby Brown calls for role on surprising TV hit: "I'd be really good"
In February this year, Brown posted a cute snap of her and her daughter sitting by the sea to mark her 22nd birthday.
"22. grateful for my husband and daughter. for my family and friends. all of my animals. I am so blessed," she wrote in the caption. "Thank you for the birthday wishes. xoxo."

The couple expanded their family through adoption, similar to when they welcomed their first daughter in August 2025.
